Before you start

Students learn the difference between popular and liked, spot the quiet and loud versions of the same power moves, and name one move that's assertive without being mean. Bring scrap paper, keep it to situations with no names, and treat outing or shared photos as a same-day counselor conversation.

Every student in the room

Present every move as something any gender does, and when insults like "soft" come up, name them as power moves that police every guy, gay or straight.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can explain the difference between popular and liked, recognize the quiet and loud versions of the same power moves in any friend group, and name one assertive move they could use, for themselves or for someone on the outside. Nobody names a real person or group.

Materials

  • Scraps of paper for the anonymous yes/no cards
  • Index cards or notebooks for the private one-move reflection
  • The student page link (last slide) to share after advisory

Flow

  1. 2 minOpen: nobody said anything, everybody knew
  2. 3 minPopular or liked? (thumbs vote)
  3. 4 minSame game, different moves (discussion)
  4. 3 minWhy nobody says anything (anonymous yes/no cards)
  5. 2 minNot a doormat, not a bully: assertive
  6. 4 minThree moments (pairs)
  7. 2 minOne move (private) and the student page

Short on time (10-minute check-in)

Popular or liked? thumbs vote (3), anonymous yes/no cards (3), one moment in pairs, Maya or Dev (3), one move and the student page link (1). The student page has the rest of the moves and what to do if you're on the outside.

Before you teach
Situations only, never names.

Keep every example about situations on the slides. Don't let students name classmates, groups or chats, and don't ask anyone where they sit or who they're with. Your advisory is a friend group too, and someone in the circle may be on the outside right now, maybe with the people doing it sitting across from them.

Leave a way back for the one who's done it.

Some students will recognize themselves as the one running the side chat. Keep shame out of it so they can use what they hear: change one thing, and keep the apology short. "I left you out, and that wasn't okay. I'm sorry."

Know what goes to a counselor the same day.

Someone being outed, photos of a person (real or AI-made) being shared, threats, or the same student targeted for weeks. Also a student who is dreading school, not eating or not sleeping because of a group. Don't ask about any of this in the circle. If a student brings up a real situation, thank them, say you'd like to help privately, and follow up with a counselor that day.

Outing is one of the most harmful moves there is.

If a student's gender identity or orientation is being spread around, treat it as urgent and private, never a discussion topic. Know where to point students: a counselor, The Trevor Project (call 1-866-488-7386 or text START to 678-678), and Trans Lifeline (877-565-8860).

When the talk turns to "girls are like this."

Or "guys are like this." Bring in the research: across 148 studies the gender difference was trivial, and most people of every gender don't run their friendships this way. Students who hear their group mocked will stop talking.

No self-harm questions in the circle.

Being shut out can hit hard. If a student says something that worries you, check in privately after advisory and walk them to a counselor. Any disclosure goes to a counselor, and 988 (call or text) is open any time.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Every gender plays, and none is the villain.

Present the quiet moves and the loud moves as patterns that show up in any group. Girls can be loud, competitive and ambitious; guys can be gentle and close with their friends. If the circle starts sorting people into "mean girls" and "meathead guys," say so and point back to the 148 studies.

Trans and nonbinary students can land outside both scripts.

Many friend groups are quietly sorted by gender, so a trans or nonbinary student may feel the group deciding which "side" they belong on. Don't ask anyone to speak for that experience. Use the scenarios as written and keep identity talk general.

"Soft" and anti-gay insults are power moves.

Pascoe found these words were used mostly to police who counts as a "real guy," whatever anyone's orientation. Name that plainly so gay, bi and questioning students hear the adult in the room treat it as a power move.

Loyalty means different things in different families.

In some families friends become family; in others private things stay private. Avoid "In X families" generalizations. Ask students what they were taught about loyalty, privately, and treat every answer as valid. Students of color in a mostly white grade, and students new to Beaver or new to the country, may carry extra pressure to fit the group's idea of how to act.

Groups often form around money.

Prom groups, formal tables, rides and weekend plans can quietly sort people by who has a car or spending money. "Keep more than one circle" includes a job, cousins, a youth group or online friends, so students who work or care for siblings hear their circles counted.

The freeze-out is harder for some students to read.

Autistic students and students with social anxiety may miss quiet cues, or read every silence as rejection. Say that asking the person directly ("Is something going on with us?") is a strong move for everyone. Let students show a thumbs vote at their desk, without having to speak.

What the research says

When students name who is popular and who they like, the lists overlap but don't match. Perceived popularity and being liked are two separate measures.

Parkhurst and Hopmeyer, Journal of Early Adolescence, 1998

Following about 300 students every year from 5th to 12th grade, researchers found that leaving people out and spreading rumors raised how popular a student seemed and lowered how much they were liked. The trade-off was strongest for girls and peaked during the move to high school.

Cillessen and Borch, Journal of Adolescence, 2006

Hurting someone through their relationships instead of with fists was named relational aggression in 1995.

Crick and Grotpeter, Child Development, 1995

A review of 148 studies and about 74,000 kids found girls use relational aggression only slightly more than boys, a difference the authors called trivial. Boys also fight physically more.

Card, Stucky, Sawalani and Little, Child Development, 2008

In 18 months at a California high school, a sociologist found guys used anti-gay insults mostly to police who counted as a "real guy," whatever anyone's orientation.

Pascoe, Dude, You're a F*g, 2007

Kids who chased status at 13 by acting older were seen as cool. By their early 20s they had more trouble in close relationships and more problems with alcohol, drugs and the law than their peers.

Allen, Schad, Oudekerk and Chango, Child Development, 2014

When other players stopped throwing to them in an online game of catch, people showed activity in a brain area that also responds to physical pain, and it tracked how upset they felt. Scientists still debate how close the overlap is.

Eisenberger, Lieberman and Williams, Science, 2003

In recorded recess observations, other kids were around for 88% of bullying episodes and stepped in during 19%. When someone stepped in, the bullying stopped 57% of the time.

Hawkins, Pepler and Craig, Social Development, 2001
